From posture to root cause: Investigate OpenShift compliance with Elastic Agent Builder
articles.context: On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete)
articles.full_text:
A single Elastic Agent on each cluster polls OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs every 60 seconds. An Elastic Agent Builder agent on top of that data can tell you what change failed the compliance control. Every scan and check result lands in Elasticsearch, as do the remediations, so the agent answers questions (like, Which clusters failed checks this week? Why did a control start failing, and when?) in plain English. The rules that the scanner marks as manual get evaluated with Common Expression Language (CEL) custom rules, and a scheduled workflow in Elastic Workflows annotates the result back to the manual rule in the cluster. Rescans and remediation patches run through those same workflows and pause for your approval. Everything in this post is on GitHub, including the integration package and workflows, along with the manifests.

The Compliance Operator scans each OpenShift cluster against configured profiles covering the CIS Benchmarks, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53 moderate (the basis for Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program [FedRAMP] authorization), the Australian Essential Eight and more, and then stores the results on that cluster. For one cluster, that’s fine, but across a fleet, nobody has a single view. A rule that passed last week starts failing after a deployment, and a scheduled scan silently fails to trigger. But the only way to find out is to log in and run oc get compliancecheckresult cluster by cluster.

Why OpenShift compliance is hard to track across a fleet

Scan results stored on each cluster

The Compliance Operator runs scans on each OpenShift cluster and stores the results locally. This approach works across a few clusters, but as the fleet grows, it becomes difficult for OpenShift administrators to maintain visibility across each cluster.

A compliance rule that had previously passed might start to fail after a new workload deployment or a cluster upgrade. Similarly, a scheduled scan can fail to trigger, due to unresolved dependencies. Without a central view of compliance scan status and results, these failures go unnoticed until an OpenShift administrator logs in to the cluster and manually checks, using commands such as oc get compliancecheckresult and oc get compliancescan.

In this blog post, we explore how this challenge can be addressed by ingesting OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch, giving platform and security teams a unified way to track compliance posture and investigate drift across the fleet.

Manual compliance rules tracked outside the cluster

Not all compliance rules are automated, so they need a manual assessment. Platform teams usually track these rules and their status in shared spreadsheets or Confluence pages. Those trackers sit apart from the scan results, and someone has to update and reconcile them with each cluster’s findings.

Organizational controls add another layer. A team may exclude certain controls from specific clusters because of internal requirements or operational needs. Without a central record, it’s hard to determine which controls apply to which cluster and why an exception exists, and that’s exactly what an auditor will ask.

Compliance reporting spread across clusters

With scan results spread across clusters, security teams have to find their own way to aggregate the data before they can build a report. Auditors can ask for reports at regular intervals, so this aggregation repeats every cycle. Each report draws on scan output and manual rule status, along with documented exceptions that live in different places. Pulling all of that together can leave gaps.

Centralizing OpenShift compliance data in Elasticsearch

Elastic Agent Builder lets you build interactive AI agents on top of your compliance data. Teams can query compliance posture across their entire fleet in plain English, investigate why specific controls failed, and safely trigger remediations with human-in-the-loop approvals, rather than combing through endless scan JSON or switching between cluster consoles.

A custom Elastic integration collects compliance scan data from each cluster and sends it to Elasticsearch. It uses the HTTP JSON input to query the OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs and retrieve scan results, in addition to ingesting them into Elasticsearch. During ingestion, compliance data is parsed and normalized, making it easier to search, build dashboards, set up alerts, and generate compliance reports.

With the data centralized, the next step is to make it easy for platform and security teams to work with it. Together, the integration and the agent turn compliance data into something that teams can interact with directly instead of static dashboards. The agent helps the team to find the information it needs and decide what to investigate next.

The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of the entire workflow discussed in this solution:

Note: The proof of concept (PoC) in this solution has been tested with OpenShift Local version 4.22, Compliance Operator 1.10.0, and Elastic Serverless. On Elastic Stack deployments (self-managed or Elastic Cloud Hosted [ECH]), both Agent Builder and Workflows require version 9.5 or later and an Enterprise subscription. On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete).

Elastic also offers a free, 14-day Elastic Cloud trial to help you get started.

How to ingest OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch

We deploy Elastic Agent directly on each OpenShift cluster using a single integration policy. Every 60 seconds, the agent queries the Compliance Operator API endpoints via HTTP JSON and ships the raw scan records into Elasticsearch data streams across your entire fleet.

The integration reads three Compliance Operator resources:

Resource / API

What it provides

compliancescans.compliance.openshift.io

The scans configured in the cluster, including scan name, phase, and result.

compliancecheckresults.compliance.openshift.io

Individual check details, including rule name, status, and severity.

complianceremediations.compliance.openshift.io

Available remediations for checks, including their current state.

Because the HTTP JSON integration appends time-series documents to a data stream on every polling cycle, three Elasticsearch transforms (scans, checks, and remedy) continuously collapse each stream into dedicated latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_-latest). The checks transform deduplicates events by cluster and check resource name (metadata.name). This ensures that checks evaluated across different node roles (such as master and worker) are preserved without creating duplicate records across repeated scan cycles.

The agent queries these latest-state indices for current posture and uses the raw time-series data streams for historical investigations.

The following diagram illustrates the compliance scan data ingestion workflow from multiple OpenShift clusters into Elastic:

Note: This is a custom-built integration and isn’t officially supported by Elastic Support.

Deploy the OpenShift compliance integration in Kibana

The custom integration is a zip file package that has all the required components. To deploy the package, you can upload the package directly using Kibana UI.

The integration follows the standard Elastic package specification and bundles all the required Kibana and Elasticsearch assets into a single archive. When uploaded through the Kibana UI, the package registers three data streams with dedicated ingest pipelines, configures prebuilt dashboards, sets up latest-state index views, and installs the continuous Elasticsearch transforms that maintain current compliance posture:

OpenShift Security Posture Management │ ├── 1. Dashboards (kibana/dashboard/) │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Posture Overview │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Overall Results │ └── [OpenShift Compliance] Auto Remediations │ ├── 2. Data Views / Index Patterns (kibana/index_pattern/) │ ├── ospm-compliance-*-latest │ └── logs-openshift_security_posture_management.compliance* │ ├── 3. Data Streams (data_stream/) │ ├── compliance_check_results (with Ingest Pipeline) │ ├── compliance_scans (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── compliance_remediations (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── 4. Elasticsearch Transforms (elasticsearch/transform/) ├── checks ├── remedy └── scans

Download the integration from the GitHub repository.

The video below walks through deploying and configuring the custom OpenShift Security Posture Management (OSPM) integration package in Kibana Fleet. It covers setting the three compliance endpoints for scans, check results, and remediations, setting the 60-second polling interval, and mapping the orchestrator.cluster.name field from the agent's environment variables.

Configure the Compliance Operator API endpoints and polling interval

The integration has three data collection endpoints that cover compliance scans, check results, and remediations. Each endpoint builds the OpenShift API URL from environment variables that Kubernetes sets in the pod, so the same configuration works on every cluster.

For compliance check results, the URL looks like this:

https://${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST}:${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT_HTTPS}/apis/compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1/compliancecheckresults

The integration polls each endpoint every 60 seconds by default. You can change the interval to match how fresh you need the data to be.

When the configuration is complete, create an Elastic Agent policy with these settings and deploy it on your OpenShift cluster to start collecting compliance data.

Deploy Elastic Agent on each OpenShift cluster

To deploy the agent and the integration:

In Kibana, create or update an Elastic Agent policy and add the OSPM integration to it. Confirm that the API endpoints and polling interval match your environment.

The integration automatically enriches each event with orchestrator.cluster.name using the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable configured on the agent.

Generate an enrollment token to be passed along with the Fleet URL endpoint.

Replace the token and Fleet URL in the following reference YAML, and deploy the Elastic Agent on the cluster.

In Fleet, check that the agent is healthy.

Once healthy, add the OSPM integration policy to the agent to start polling data.

In Kibana, open the integration’s data streams. Confirm that documents are arriving and that each one carries the expected cluster name in orchestrator.cluster.name.

Repeat these steps for every OpenShift cluster that you want to monitor, and set the matching cluster name for each environment.

To collect OpenShift compliance data, deploy Elastic Agent as a single-replica deployment on each OpenShift cluster. The manifest below runs the agent with Fleet enrollment enabled and mounts a persistent volume to preserve agent state across pod restarts. It also injects the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable. The integration uses this variable to tag every ingested event with orchestrator.cluster.name, ensuring that multi-cluster scan results remain separated in Elasticsearch.

--- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: elastic-agent namespace: elastic-agent-ocp labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent template: metadata: labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: elastic-agent spec: serviceAccountName: elastic-agent containers: - name: elastic-agent image: docker.elastic.co/elastic-agent/elastic-agent:9.5.5 env: - name: CLUSTER_NAME value: "<Replace-cluster-name>" #replace this with your actual cluster name # Set to 1 for enrollment into Fleet server. If not set, Elastic Agent runs standalone. - name: FLEET_ENROLL value: "1" # Set to true to communicate with Fleet with either insecure HTTP or unverified HTTPS. - name: FLEET_INSECURE value: "false" # Fleet Server URL to enroll the Elastic Agent into. # Found in Kibana: Management > Fleet > Settings. - name: FLEET_URL value: "<Replace-fleet-url>" # Enrollment token used to enroll the Elastic Agent in Fleet. - name: FLEET_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN value: "<replace-token>" resources: limits: memory: 500Mi requests: cpu: 100m memory: 200Mi volumeMounts: # Persist Elastic Agent state across pod restarts within the pod's lifetime. - name: elastic-agent-state mountPath: /usr/share/elastic-agent/state volumes: - name: elastic-agent-state persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: agent-state

Note: The above manifest is to deploy a single replica elastic agent pod to scan and ingest compliance data. For OpenShift cluster logs and metrics, use the Elastic Kubernetes integration separately.

Complete Kubernetes manifests and role-based access control (RBAC) are available in the GitHub repository.

How to automate manual OpenShift compliance rules with CEL

Starting with Red Hat OpenShift Compliance Operator version 1.10.0, CEL-based custom rules are generally available (GA). Using this feature, create a CustomRule object for rules tagged as Manual.

For example, the compliance rule accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens is common across the profiles ocp4-cis and ocp4-high. Using a CEL expression, check whether any pods have the property spec.automountServiceAccountToken set to true:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: CustomRule metadata: name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens namespace: openshift-compliance spec: id: xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_accounts_restrict_service_account_tokens title: "Service account tokens should not be automounted unless required" severity: medium checkType: Platform scannerType: CEL expression: | pods.items.all(p, !has(p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken) || p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken == false ) failureReason: "A pod has automountServiceAccountToken set to true" inputs: - name: pods kubernetesInputSpec: apiVersion: v1 resource: pods

Note: In the custom rule above, spec.id is mapped the same as in the original rule with status of Manual.

Custom rules cannot be evaluated directly on their own; they must be enabled through a TailoredProfile object. To execute the checks, bind this TailoredProfile to a ScanSetting using a ScanSettingBinding.

For example, create a TailoredProfile named custom-ocp4-manual-rules for the custom CEL rule custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: TailoredProfile metadata: name: custom-ocp4-manual-rules namespace: openshift-compliance spec: title: "Custom CEL automation for shared manual rules (cis/e8/high)" description: "Each rule is evaluated once; rationale documents which native profiles it should be patched back to." enableRules: - name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens kind: CustomRule rationale: "applies-to: cis,high"

Using a similar pattern, CEL checks for all the rules tagged as MANUAL can be evaluated.

Note: CEL-based evaluation only supports platform type rules.

In the Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions section, we define a workflow that reads scan data from these custom rules ingested into Elasticsearch and uses it to annotate MANUAL rules on the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) cluster based on their custom scan status. Because the OpenShift Compliance Operator automatically propagates custom annotations from Rule custom resources (CRs) to their corresponding ComplianceCheckResult objects during scan runs, these evaluated statuses are automatically ingested into Elasticsearch on the subsequent scan cycle.

The following diagram illustrates the sequence for evaluating MANUAL compliance rules using a CEL-based check and annotating the result to the actual rule:

Build the OpenShift compliance agent in Agent Builder

Agent Builder lets you build purpose-driven AI agents connected to your Elasticsearch data. It provides four core building blocks (instructions, skills, tools, and connectors) that govern how the agent reasons and queries data, along with how it interacts with external platforms.

In this post, we build a custom OpenShift compliance agent, which reviews compliance scan data and identifies noncompliant clusters. It also evaluates failed compliance rules. Using tools, it can also trigger compliance scans and apply auto-remediation patches. Plus, it can generate operational reports.

The goal of this compliance agent is to let platform and security teams query compliance data in natural language, without writing custom queries or manually correlating results across clusters.

The following diagram illustrates the anatomy of the OpenShift compliance agent:

Set the compliance agent’s instructions and guardrails

Configuring an agent in Agent Builder starts with custom instructions, which become part of the system prompt. They set the persona and reasoning habits for everything the agent does, in addition to the guardrails. For an OpenShift compliance agent, the most important decision is what level of actions the agent is allowed to perform. This agent uses a strictly precautionary role. It reviews and queries ingested compliance data and can apply remediation patches or trigger scans on the cluster with user approval. It treats the data in Elasticsearch as the source of truth and asks for any unstated detail, such as the cluster name or scan identifier, rather than assuming defaults.

The instructions are structured in Markdown across six focused sections (goal, steps, guardrails, domain context, output conventions, and edge cases):

Section

What it covers

Goal

The agent only handles OpenShift compliance; the ingested Elasticsearch data is the source of truth.

Steps

Confirm scope, retrieve data with the provided tools, verify the results, summarize, and then ask before acting.

Guardrails

No change without explicit approval; only the provided tools; no invented IDs or remediation; and off-topic requests are declined.

Domain context

Rules that the model cannot infer from the data, such as the custom scan and how manual checks are reported.

Output conventions

Timestamps in local time, plus the ingested and original timestamps for Elasticsearch data; sources are cited.

Edge cases

Missing input means ask; a failed or empty tool result is stated, never read as "compliant."

This excerpt from the directives and guardrails shows the tone:

# Guardrails - **Cluster Mapping**: Cluster name provided by the user must match orchestrator.cluster.name exactly as recorded in compliance data. - **Silent Exclusion of Custom Scans**: By default, completely omit and suppress any scan or check result where scan_name contains custom (case-insensitive *custom*). Do NOT list, mention, or show an "Excluded custom scans" section or table in the output. Filter them out completely silently. Only include them if the user explicitly requests custom scans. - **Handling Manual Rules**: Treat OpenShift's base status MANUAL as manual review. If a custom automated evaluation exists, read manual_scan_status (PASS/FAIL) and last_manual_scan timestamp and report that custom evaluation separately. If absent, report "no manual scan annotation recorded". - **Strict Read-Only Workload Investigation**: When investigating which workload or pod caused a rule to fail, the agent operates in strictly read-only mode. The agent must NEVER mutate, patch, or change application workloads. It identifies the root cause and user attribution, and provides the remediation steps for the OpenShift administrator to execute. - **Safety**: Never execute live cluster changes or scans without presenting the plan and receiving explicit user confirmation. - **Concise Communication**: Answer directly and concisely using clear Markdown tables. Do not ask follow-up questions or offer unsolicited next steps unless clarification is strictly necessary to answer the prompt.

The instructions also carry domain context that a model cannot infer from the data. In OpenShift clusters, a custom scan bound to the custom-ocp4-manual-rules tailored profile tests manual rules. The agent leaves it out of summaries and counts unless the user asks for it.

For manual checks in the other scans, the agent reports two statuses side by side: the original status (MANUAL); and the manual scan status from the annotation that a scheduled Elastic workflow writes back to the cluster. Putting these rules in the instructions keeps them in one place, so no tool or skill needs to repeat them. Also, the whole block is static, with no timestamps or session IDs, so prompt caching keeps working.

Add skills for posture, failure investigation, and reporting

Custom instructions are loaded on every turn, making them ideal for general guardrails and domain context. However, adding detailed task workflows to system instructions creates unnecessary prompt overhead. Instead, define modular skills that the agent loads dynamically when the user request matches the skill description.

The OpenShift compliance agent uses four skills, each covering a single responsibility:

Skill

Reads from

What it does

Posture summary

Latest-state indices

Summarizes current scan results, pass and fail counts, failed controls by severity, manual check status, and remediation state.

Failure investigation

Raw data streams

Explains why a check failed or when it started failing, using history and remediation records. Kubernetes log correlation comes once audit logs are ingested.

Live cluster actions

Live cluster, through workflows

Reads live state, triggers a rescan, and applies or reverts a remediation, always after user approval.

Reporting

Latest and raw data

Produces reports, trends, and scan comparisons, and creates dashboards after user approves.

Each skill includes a description specifying its purpose and trigger criteria. Below is the description for the Posture Summary skill:

Summarize OpenShift compliance posture, scan execution status, check results, manual rule evaluations, and remediation states from latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_*-latest).

Each skill defines its own trigger conditions, available tools, workflow rules, and decision trees, along with output standards, execution steps, examples, and edge cases. For example, the manual check logic described in the previous section is implemented as:

Manual Rules & Custom Automated Evaluations When manual rules are requested, call ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status with status: "MANUAL". For every manual check, inspect both the base OpenShift status and the custom evaluation annotations: Report the base status as MANUAL. If manual_scan_status contains a value (e.g. PASS or FAIL), present it separately as: "Custom Evaluation Status: (last evaluated at <last_manual_scan>)". If both manual_scan_status and last_manual_scan are empty/null, explicitly state: "No manual scan annotation recorded" (indicating it still requires manual verification). Do not interpret or alter values beyond what the data fields show.

Custom ES|QL tools for querying compliance data

Skills tell the agent how to approach a task, but executing those steps requires tools to query data and perform actions. Because compliance scan data is normalized and stored in Elasticsearch, the agent uses targeted tools to search current posture and historical trends. Following are the tools configured for the compliance agent:

Tool

Type

What it does

ocp_compliance.get_scan_status

Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL)

Lists the scans on a cluster with result, phase, and timestamps.

ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status

ES|QL

Lists checks with a given status, including manual scan annotations for manual checks.

ocp_compliance.list_remediations

ES|QL

Lists auto remediations with their apply flag, state, and target object.

ocp_compliance.get_rule_details

ES|QL

Looks up a specific compliance rule from latest-state data.

ocp_compliance.search_audit_logs

Index search

Searches the OpenShift cluster audit logs ingested into Elasticsearch cluster.

ocp_compliance.search_compliance_history

Index search

Offers open-ended search over the raw event history.

Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions

Although large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning and synthesis, you don't want an AI model improvising arbitrary mutations against a live OpenShift cluster. Elastic Workflows solves this by executing deterministic, YAML-defined steps that run identically every time. When exposed to Agent Builder as tools, the agent decides when to invoke a workflow based on your prompt but cannot alter its underlying execution logic, ensuring strict guardrails around cluster interactions.

Four workflows handle the live cluster interactions supported by the agent, alongside a scheduled automation workflow that reconciles manual rule annotations:

Workflow name

Agent tool

What it does

openshift-compliance-query-live-workload

ocp_compliance.query_live_workload

Executes a strictly read-only HTTP GET request against the live OpenShift API to inspect objects and pinpoint the offending resource.

openshift-compliance-read-live-state

ocp_compliance.live_read_state

Reads the live state of one ComplianceScan, ComplianceCheckResult, or ComplianceRemediation directly from the OpenShift API.

openshift-compliance-trigger-scan

ocp_compliance.trigger_scan

Reruns an existing ComplianceScan on the live cluster by setting the rescan annotation.

openshift-compliance-set-remediation-state

ocp_compliance.set_remediation_state

Applies (apply: true) or reverts a native ComplianceRemediation on the live cluster.

Annotate custom compliance Rule resources

N/A

Checks custom CEL rule outcomes in Elasticsearch and annotates the corresponding rule object on the OpenShift cluster.

Each workflow tool has Require user confirmation set to Always, so Agent Builder pauses and asks to approve every call.

Connect Elastic to the OpenShift API with the Kubernetes connector

The Elastic Kubernetes connector provides secure connectivity between the Elastic Stack and OpenShift API endpoints, allowing workflows to interact directly with cluster resources.

The service account token configured for the connector must follow the principle of least privilege, scoped strictly to the operations required by the workflows.

The connector needs patch permissions on the Compliance Operator custom resource definitions (CRDs), so workflows can trigger scans and apply remediations. Investigations need more than that; the agent has to read pods and service accounts, along with RBAC bindings, to find the workload behind a failed check, which also means read-only access to cluster workloads. You can grant both in two ways:

Approach

Permissions granted

When to use

Dedicated connector service account

Bound to the OpenShift view or cluster-reader ClusterRole for read-only workload queries, plus a scoped role granting patch on compliancescans and complianceremediations in compliance.openshift.io.

Production. The connector’s access is separate from the agent’s and can be audited and revoked on its own.

Extend the existing agent service account

Adds get and list on pods, serviceaccounts, and rolebindings to the existing elastic-agent-ospm ClusterRole.

PoCs and lab environments, where standing up a second service account is more setup than the exercise warrants.

The example below generates a token for the existing elastic-agent service account:

oc create token elastic-agent -n elastic-agent-ocp --duration=720h

Note: When deploying across multiple clusters or staging environments, ensure that connector-id in the workflow matches the specific Kubernetes connector configured for that cluster.

The complete OpenShift compliance agent architecture

OpenShift compliance agent demo: From failed control to root cause

The demo below follows the OpenShift compliance agent across an end-to-end investigation scenario. It shows how the agent summarizes multi-cluster posture and flags rule failures. It also demonstrates how the agent uses Elastic Workflows to query live pods without leaving the chat interface. From there, the agent correlates OpenShift audit logs in Elasticsearch to trace the exact user and deployment that caused the policy drift and documents the timeline into an Elastic case. And it shows how execution guardrails block unauthorized or destructive cluster commands.

Conclusion: OpenShift compliance monitoring at fleet scale

The OpenShift Compliance Operator does the essential work of auditing cluster configurations, but keeping a multi-cluster fleet compliant shouldn't require juggling spreadsheets or hunting down failed pods manually, nor should it force you to scramble before every audit.

Centralizing compliance findings in Elasticsearch and putting Agent Builder on top shifts the experience from static dashboards to active, evidence-backed investigation. Teams can query posture across clusters in plain English and automate manual checks with CEL and scheduled workflows. They can also trace policy drift down to the exact OpenShift user and timestamp, all while keeping humans firmly in control of live cluster changes.

articles.title: European Commission Cyberattack: ARTEX AI Tool Suspected in Prolonged Disruption
articles.context: A cyberattack disrupted EU Commission services for over ten days
articles.full_text:
A cyberattack disrupted EU Commission services for over ten days. ARTEX is suspected, while investigators assess whether staff data was stolen.

A cyberattack has disrupted internal European Commission systems for more than ten days, hitting payroll, leave requests and medical reimbursements. Politico’s Brussels Playbook reports the Corporate Management Board, the Commission’s top internal crisis body, met urgently over the incident, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed the full College of Commissioners on 18 November. An EU official told Politico the Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, while the full extent of any damage remains unclear.

Sysper, the HR platform for payslips, timesheets and leave, crashed briefly again on 18 November after access had been restored earlier in the week. MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, came back online around the same time. JSIS, the staff health insurance portal, was still down on 19 November according to a Commission employee cited by Euronews, and translation services went offline on 17 November, prompting one official to admit to “swearing a lot.”

Pay still landed on time, according to staff Politico spoke to, even as some couldn’t submit timesheets or request leave. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed the response to Politico: “Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

Some staff still complained the internal communication said little, and an IT reply about the Sysper problem cited a general technical issue without mentioning an attack.

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team that protects EU institutions, detected the activity and identified ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing tool, as a possible tool used in the attack. An EU official told Politico that some threat actors misuse tools like ARTEX and have targeted the Commission. In a technical note published on 5 November, CERT-EU described ARTEX as a system that uses AI agents. An operator gives it an objective in plain language, and the software breaks it down into smaller tasks that the agents carry out using real hacking tools.

ARTEX does not include its own AI model. Instead, it connects to an external AI model selected by the operator. Its original developer removed the project from its repository in October after reports of misuse. However, independent copies are still available, so removing the original project does not prevent others from using it. So far, there is no public information explaining how the attackers entered the Commission’s systems. The reference to ARTEX therefore points to a suspected tool, not a confirmed attack method or the identity of those responsible.

The biggest unanswered question is whether staff data was stolen. This could include names, salary details, home addresses or health information. Investigators have not yet confirmed whether anyone accessed this data, which explains why the Commission has shared little information with employees.

Taking systems offline or restoring them does not prove that no data was stolen. Getting a service back online only shows that it is working again. It does not mean attackers did not copy information before the system was shut down.

Under EU Regulation 2018/1725, a confirmed personal data breach must normally be reported to the European Data Protection Supervisor within 72 hours. If the breach creates a high risk for individuals, they must also be informed without delay. However, these deadlines only start once a personal data breach has been confirmed.

This is not the Commission’s first security incident this year, although no link between the cases has been established. On January 30, attackers left traces in the system used to manage staff mobile devices. Some names and phone numbers were exposed. The Commission said it contained and cleaned up the incident within nine hours.

A more serious incident happened in March. Attackers compromised a software update for Trivy, a security tool, and used it to enter an AWS cloud environment. They stole around 91.7 GB of compressed data, including personal information and email content. The breach may also have affected at least 29 other EU institutions and bodies.

The timeline shows that the Commission restored its systems before it fully understood what had happened. Services came back online in stages, but key questions remain unanswered: where did the attack start, which systems were affected, and was any data stolen, and who is behind the attack?

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, European Commission)

articles.title: European Commission Confirms AI-Driven Cyber-Attack Took Systems Offline
articles.context: He said the intrusion was detected on October 22, 2026, and confirmed as a cyber-attack on October 26, which triggered mitigation steps being carried out and an investigation...
articles.full_text:
The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by an AI-driven cyber-attack that resulted in services being taken offline.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier revealed the incident during a press briefing on November 19. He said the intrusion was detected on October 22, 2026, and confirmed as a cyber-attack on October 26, which triggered mitigation steps being carried out and an investigation launched.

“I can confirm that the Commission has recently taken necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign. As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored,” Regnier said in response to a journalist question.

No information was given as to the potential perpetrators of the attack, or whether any data was accessed during the incident, with Regnier stating that the investigation was ongoing in response to questions on these points.

However, he said he was “not aware” of a ransomware demand being issued to the Commission and that the investigation has not detected “any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.”

Regnier added that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) has been notified about the attack.

In a statement emailed to Infosecurity after the press conference, a Commission spokesperson said the attack targeted “individual systems,” with impacted teams informed in line with standard practice.

“The Commission has been working to strengthen the security of its systems and continues to take appropriate measures. We are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS. The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings,” the spokesperson continued.

The comments follow a report published earlier in the day by Politico that the European Commission had been hit by a cyber-attack which may have breached the personal information of employees, and resulted in a number of systems being taken offline.

These included Sysper, an HR platform used by EU Commission staff members for payslips and time management and a system for medical reimbursements.

Commission Attack “AI Generated”

Regnier confirmed that the attack was “AI generated” involving the use of a “publicly available” tool.

“We have seen many global cyber-attacks recently and of course no one is immune to this, AI assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities. Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools,” he said.

The Politico article claimed the attack had been launched using the Chinese AI penetration-testing tool ARTEX, which is believed to be widely used in campaigns over recent months.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

On November 5, CERT-EU, the EU’s cybersecurity emergency response team, warned that it had observed several threat actors around the world using ARTEX to automate their campaigns.

Similarly, an FBI Flash notice published on November 13 noted that a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally since at least August 2026.

Commenting on the incident, Chris Dimitriadis, chief global strategy officer at ISACA, warned that AI is enabling attackers to hack “at the speed of intent”, which organizations from all sectors cannot keep pace with.

“Until organizations deploy AI defensively as fast as criminals deploy it aggressively, we will continue on this trajectory,” he said.

“In the short term, the Commission will investigate whether staff data has been compromised and what weakness hackers were able to use ARTEX to exploit. They should be bolstering their cybersecurity and building long-term resilience by investing in recruiting, training, and upskilling privacy professionals who can build defenses that are stronger than the AI tools now freely available to attackers.”

articles.title: Ukraine, FBI arrest ransomware gang members tied to $40M in ransoms
articles.context: The attackers researched their victims' financial standing, assets, employees, and IT vulnerabilities before launching attacks designed to steal corporate data, encrypt systems,...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian authorities, working with the FBI, have arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware organization linked to more than $40.5 million in ransom payments from at least 28 companies worldwide.

The arrests come after a two-year investigation into a cybercrime organization comprising at least 27 individuals from Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Russia, and other countries.

Investigators say the organization was connected to a larger cybercrime network of more than 60 members operating across eight jurisdictions, including former members of the notorious Conti ransomware gang.

According to Ukraine's National Police, the group targeted organizations in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing, logistics, and financial sectors, as well as critical infrastructure.

The attackers researched their victims' financial standing, assets, employees, and IT vulnerabilities before launching attacks designed to steal corporate data, encrypt systems, and extort cryptocurrency payments.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with Ukrainian news outlet Censor.NET, acting National Police chief Maksym Tsutskiridze said investigators had identified at least 28 companies that paid more than $40.5 million in ransoms.

"We have identified at least 28 companies that transferred more than $40.5 million in ransom payments to the hackers, equivalent to approximately UAH 1.8 billion. This is money that has already been paid. We are still establishing the full extent of the damage," Tsutskiridze said.

In one attack, the hackers stole 1.4 terabytes of data from a U.S. company and expanded their attack to other companies within the same corporate group.

The attackers initially demanded $10 million but ultimately received $5 million after negotiations.

As first reported by French cybersecurity news outlet LeMagIT, Ukrainian court records identify several victims of the criminal organization, including Warren Oil Company, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources, and Quantum Health.

The court documents identify Warren Oil Company as the victim of an August 2024 attack in which hackers copied 1.4 TB of data before receiving an 84.5 BTC ransom payment, equivalent to approximately $5 million at the time.

The records also allege that Newpark Resources paid $1.5 million in December 2024, while Quantum Health paid $5 million in June 2026 following an initial $15 million ransom demand.

LeMagIT also noted that the BlackSuit ransomware gang claimed Maxxis International as a victim in November 2024, while Ukrainian court records identify Chaos as the ransomware used by the criminal organization.

The Conti ransomware operation shut down in May 2022, with its members dispersing into smaller ransomware gangs and other cybercrime operations.

One of the groups linked to former Conti members was BlackSuit, which initially operated as Quantum ransomware in January 2022 before becoming Royal.

In June 2023, Royal began operating under the BlackSuit name after testing a new encryptor and carrying out high-profile attacks, including one against the City of Dallas, Texas.

However, Ukrainian authorities have not identified the four arrested suspects as former Conti members or confirmed their individual affiliations with BlackSuit or Chaos.

AI-powered IT support impersonation

To breach corporate networks, the cybercriminals impersonated IT support personnel and used a custom-developed platform with AI-generated voice messages to automate fraudulent phone calls.

During these calls, they tricked employees into disclosing login credentials or installing remote-access software, allowing the attackers to access internal corporate systems.

In one documented incident, an attacker kept an employee on the phone while another attacker accessed the company's systems, with the call ending only after the attackers confirmed the intrusion was successful.

"They created their own platform featuring voice messages generated by artificial intelligence. They called company employees, posing as IT support specialists. Under the pretext of providing technical assistance, they persuaded employees to disclose their login credentials or install remote access software. This allowed them to gain access to corporate networks," Tsutskiridze explained.

The Ukrainian court records provide additional insight into these attacks, describing how the hackers used phishing pages impersonating corporate VPN services, spoofed phone numbers, and remote-access tools such as TeamViewer and AnyDesk.

During the Warren Oil Company attack, the records allege that the attackers tricked an employee into entering credentials on a phishing page, then obtained a two-factor authentication code that granted them remote access to the corporate network.

Once inside the network, the attackers stole sensitive information and encrypted files using ransomware, disrupting the victim's operations.

The gang then demanded cryptocurrency payments in exchange for restoring access to encrypted systems while threatening to publicly release stolen corporate data.

"They would deprive a company of access to its own data and then demand millions of dollars in exchange for decrypting it. At the same time, they threatened to publish the stolen information. Victims were put under pressure from both sides, forcing them to pay the ransom in cryptocurrency," Tsutskiridze said.

Ukrainian authorities conducted 66 simultaneous searches across Kyiv and 11 regions of Ukraine as part of the joint operation with U.S. law enforcement. Four suspected key members of the organization were detained, although authorities did not disclose their exact arrest locations.

During these searches, investigators seized computers, mobile phones, bank cards, nearly $370,000 in cash, and €20,000.

Four alleged key members of the organization were formally notified of suspicion and are currently in custody.

The suspects face charges related to participating in a criminal organization and unauthorized interference with information systems under Ukrainian law. If convicted, they face up to 15 years in prison.

Ukrainian authorities say the investigation is ongoing as law enforcement works to identify additional members of the international network and determine their involvement in other cyberattacks.

The National Police also released a video showing footage from the investigation, including law enforcement raids, seized cash, interviews with investigators, and a suspect being questioned.

The video also contains audio from an alleged ransomware extortion call demanding $15 million after claiming to have stolen more than 1.5 TB of corporate data.

articles.title: Apple Services Disrupted as NSA Network Goes Down and Equinor Faces Cyberattack
articles.context: The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft
articles.full_text:
Apple and NSA services faced outages as Equinor reported a cyberattack, highlighting the risks facing increasingly connected infrastructure.

Apple customers faced widespread service problems on November 17, with issues affecting iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device.

The disruption came after a week of technical failures involving major technology companies, banking services and US government networks. At the same time, Norwegian energy company Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems.

Apple’s System Status page reported problems with iCloud Account and Sign In, affecting all users. The issue prevented customers from signing in to their Apple accounts or caused repeated requests for their Apple ID passwords. Some users also reported difficulties activating new iPhones, suggesting that the disruption was affecting essential account services, not just individual apps.

According to TechCrunch, the problems also affected the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device. Apple had not issued a detailed public explanation at the time of publication, beyond listing the incidents on its status page. The company said in a statement that the issue was caused by an internal update.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” reads the statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

The Apple outage attracted attention because it followed several other major disruptions. Microsoft had experienced a widespread failure affecting Outlook and Teams, while JPMorgan Chase customers had reported problems with online banking. A separate outage also affected the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network, known as NSANet.

The NSA incident raised particular concerns because the network supports classified communications. However, the cause and full extent of the disruption remained unclear. Reports cited by Forbes Middle East said there was no evidence that the NSA outage resulted from a cyberattack. A system patch had reportedly been underway before the disruption.

The growing number of outages does not mean they share the same cause or are part of a coordinated cyber campaign. Technical problems, software bugs, configuration errors and infrastructure failures can affect major services without any cyberattack. Claims about AI-powered attacks should not be made without evidence.

On the same day, Norway’s energy company Equinor reported a cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft. Equinor said it had activated its response teams and notified the relevant authorities. The company stated that “there were no signs data had been stolen.”

The Equinor incident added a confirmed cyberattack to a day already marked by several service outages. However, these events should not be confused. Equinor confirmed a cyberattack, while there was no evidence that the outages affecting Apple and the NSA were caused by malicious activity.

Cyberattacks can compromise systems and data, while ordinary technical failures can disrupt services that businesses, public institutions and millions of people depend on. Both require effective incident response, clear communication and the ability to maintain essential operations when technology fails.

For now, there is no evidence that the recent outages affecting Apple, Microsoft, the NSA, banks and aviation systems are connected. Nor should every major service disruption be treated as evidence of a cyberattack. As Forbes reported about the NSA incident, “there was no evidence the disruption was the result of a cyberattack.”

The distinction matters. In a period of heightened cyber threats and growing dependence on digital services, organizations need to investigate incidents carefully, communicate what they know and avoid confusing coincidence with attribution. A technical outage is not necessarily a cyberattack, but it can still expose serious weaknesses in the systems on which society depends.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)

articles.title: Using the AWS RMiT workbook and ISO Compliance Guides to support your BNM submissions
articles.context: In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services
articles.full_text:
Your next Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) notification submission needs auditable evidence of how Amazon Web Services (AWS) controls align with Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) requirements. Two resources now exist to support that work: the AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT and the compliance guides published by AWS Security Assurance Services (AWS SAS).

The AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT, available through AWS Artifact, maps each RMiT provision to AWS Control Objectives (AWS responsibilities under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model) and AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices (your responsibilities). It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement.

The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture.

Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. BNM expects this specificity in notification documentation.

AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT

The workbook is a structured Excel document available through AWS Artifact. For each of the 394 RMiT provisions, it identifies:

Whether the requirement is an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model

The specific AWS Control Objective that addresses the requirement (where AWS is responsible)

The relevant AWS Well-Architected Framework best practice for customer implementation (where the customer is responsible)

Supporting information and references for each mapping

The following is a sample entry from the workbook:

RMiT Requirement

Responsibility

Source

AWS supporting information

10.49: A financial institution should ensure network resilience…

AWS

AWS Control Objectives

AWS Control Section: Network Security. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone.

10.49: (Customer responsibility)

Customer

Well-Architected

REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall.

The workbook currently includes 394 rows across all RMiT appendix requirements, with 208 mapped to AWS responsibilities and 186 to customer responsibilities.

Why this matters now

BNM revised RMiT guidelines effective 28 November 2025, and updated them on 25 September 2026 to add requirements for National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities. Financial institutions operating under both BNM Outsourcing and BNM RMiT must demonstrate that their cloud service providers maintain controls aligned with regulatory expectations. Institutions preparing notification submissions for material cloud workloads need auditable evidence of this alignment.

The revised guidelines set higher expectations for evidence quality. Institutions submitting notifications without clear, structured control mapping evidence might face extended review cycles and requests for additional information from BNM. Workloads that could be deployed in weeks remain in governance queues for months when supporting documentation lacks the specificity regulators expect.

Compliance guides from AWS Security Assurance Services

Start with the RMiT workbook to identify which provisions AWS addresses and which you implement. Then use the following compliance guides to design and implement your customer-side controls. The guides are implementation guidance for your teams. Audit evidence comes from two places. For AWS-side controls, use AWS third-party attestations, such as ISO certificates and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports, available in AWS Artifact. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS.

AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. These guides were written by AWS SAS practicing security assessors and auditors holding Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (PCI QSA), Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), ISO 27001 Lead Auditor, and Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certifications, drawing on experience from hundreds of cloud security assessments across financial services globally.

The following is the list of guides AWS SAS practicing auditors have published, which include control mapping information relevant to BNM RMiT:

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS (Information Security Management) – Maps Annex A controls to AWS services

ISO 31000:2018 on AWS (Risk Management) – Integrates AWS services into risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) – Supports institutions building responsible artificial intelligence (AI) on AWS

Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1 on AWS (Cloud Security Controls) – Maps 207 control objectives to AWS

American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) SOC 2 on AWS – Navigates SOC 2 compliance using AWS services

How these resources work together

A Malaysian financial institution preparing a BNM notification can use these resources together:

The RMiT workbook identifies which RMiT provisions are AWS responsibilities and which are customer responsibilities.

For AWS responsibilities, the workbook references the specific AWS Control Objective.

AWS third-party reports in AWS Artifact, such as the AWS ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and SOC reports, attest to those AWS Control Objectives. For customer responsibilities, the ISO compliance guides show how to implement the corresponding controls using AWS services.

The ISO 31000 guide can inform the risk management methodology you apply to your cloud workloads.

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated, continuous monitoring of deployed controls.

Resources also supporting this approach:

The AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia examines the BNM Outsourcing and RMiT policy documents and sets out the steps to launch regulated workloads on AWS

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated compliance monitoring through managed AWS Config rules mapped to specific RMiT controls

Compliance teams across Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) financial services have already begun referencing the AWS Guide to BNM RMiT and associated resources in their cloud risk assessment processes and BNM notification documentation.

Looking ahead: AI governance

For institutions deploying generative AI and machine learning, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) is relevant to BNM technology governance expectations. In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services. AWS passed its first surveillance audit in November 2025 with zero findings. The ISO 42001 compliance guide published in May 2026 supports institutions building their own responsible AI systems on their side of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.

How to get started

Access the RMiT workbook through AWS Artifact and review with your compliance lead to identify which provisions apply to your material cloud workloads.

Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence.

Map your workload-specific controls using the workbook as the RMiT baseline and the ISO guides as implementation guidance.

Implement automated compliance monitoring using the BNM RMiT conformance pack for AWS Config to maintain continuous visibility over your control posture.

Engage your AWS account team or AWS SAS for additional guidance on implementing customer-side controls referenced in the workbook.

As BNM updates its regulatory expectations, AWS will update these resources to reflect revised requirements. Subscribe to the AWS Security Blog for update notifications.

articles.title: EU Sanctions 30 People and Two Entities Over Russian Disinformation and Cyberattacks
articles.context: 16, 2026 Help Net Security, Global crackdown hits pro-Russian cybercrime, 100+ systems taken down worldwide (Europol's Operation Eastwood), July 16, 2025 The post EU Sanctions...
articles.full_text:
On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks.

A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list.

It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign.

What the Council announced

The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes:

Russia's destabilizing activities regime, created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date.

The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime, in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities.

The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing.

Who's on the list

The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections.

The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them.

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces.

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going.

The target is the supply chain, not the operators

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze.

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains.

The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers.

The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point.

Who's affected

Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely.

The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named.

The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming.

Plan of action

Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties.

Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly.

Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name.

Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds.

Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted.

What we're watching

NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage.

Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works.

The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them.

Key takeaways

On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime.

The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly.

Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines.

Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
articles.context: The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC
articles.full_text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models.

The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged.

“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial.

Other incidents and internal breaches

In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said.

The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents.

At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. Administrators removed more than 500 packages they considered malicious, and the platform suspended new user registrations between May 12 and May 16.

The complaint also alleged that agents made approximately 17,000 edits to a German website, DseWiki, using it as a message board to exchange information about bypassing sandbox restrictions.

Other incidents involved Wikimedia Foundation’s infrastructure and Australian government websites. The complaint said agents overwhelmed Wikimedia services with millions of API requests and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries, likely contributing to a partial outage in May. In June, agents allegedly accessed non-public information from Australian government websites.

The complaint further said OpenAI notified dozens of organizations whose websites or internal systems had been accessed by its agents. These included government institutions, law enforcement agencies, educational institutions, and small businesses. Some incidents allegedly involved stolen credentials, API keys, and fraudulent accounts, with agents accessing personally identifiable information.

OpenAI’s own infrastructure was also compromised in at least three attacks in July, according to the complaint. Agents allegedly obtained administrator-level access to systems supporting cloud model deployment, secrets management, and identity and access management.

Escapes after the fix

The state argued that the danger is ongoing. On September 20, after OpenAI had hardened its environment, an agent escaped during a training run and reached an external chatbot.

“This incident occurred after OpenAI had implemented ‘security hardening’ following the Hugging Face attack,” the lawsuit added.

OpenAI detected it within minutes, but the run did not stop automatically, and human reviewers took two more hours to halt it, the complaint said.

OpenAI announced a pause on training and evaluating its most capable models on September 25. The pause lasted five days, ending October 1, according to the complaint.

Warnings that went unheeded

The complaint argued that the incidents were foreseeable. It cited the run-up to the Hugging Face attack as evidence. By May 26, agents had used a vulnerability in a misconfigured software package service to reach the public internet.

An internal OpenAI team saw at least one agent escape but apparently took no action, the complaint said. On June 27, a security monitoring tool flagged that the research environment was being probed for vulnerabilities, and OpenAI again did not stop its runs.

When agent traffic knocked the service offline on July 4, OpenAI patched it over the holiday weekend and resumed runs on July 7, the state alleged. Two days later, agents broke out again.

The state also faulted OpenAI for not running live chain-of-thought monitoring in training and evaluation, even though it did so for models deployed to employees. During the Hugging Face attack, one agent’s reasoning read: “We’re attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized.”

Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on September 30. OpenAI answered with a 14-page letter and produced no supporting documents, the complaint said.

California is not the only state pressing OpenAI. In August, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird led a 15-state coalition demanding that OpenAI preserve evidence, protect whistleblowers and halt the tests behind the hack until it could show it can run them responsibly. “The AI weaponized itself, which is extremely scary,” Bird said in a statement.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

articles.title: ICO Issues GTA 6 Scam Warning as Release Date Nears
articles.context: The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of...
articles.full_text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6).

The much-anticipated title is set to launch worldwide on November 19, but the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) urged caution when opening messages with GTA 6 themes.

These could be crafted to steal passwords that are used to log into victims’ gaming accounts and other online accounts that share the same credentials.

The ICO said that email inboxes, financial information and other personal details could be at risk.

Read more on ICO advice: ICO Publishes Five-Step Plan to Counter Emerging AI-Powered Attacks.

“Phishing emails and other cyber vulnerabilities can be used to access people's personal information. And if you’re using the same password across multiple accounts, one mistake could give criminals the keys to much more than your gaming profile,” said ICO group director – regulatory assurance and cyber, Ian Hulme.

“Our message is simple: enjoy the game, but protect your data. Use unique passwords, switch on two-step verification for your accounts and think carefully before clicking links or sharing personal information.”

Five Steps to Protect Personal Information

The ICO’s advice for GTA 6 fans is useful best practice for any computer user. It urges individuals to:

Use different passwords across multiple accounts to reduce the blast radius of an attack if a scammer gets hold of one

Choose passwords carefully, avoiding those based on personal information such as a pet’s name or date of birth. Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, long and unique passwords

Be wary of suspicious links in unsolicited messages or emails – especially those promising free downloads, exclusive content or early access

Think before sharing personal information online, including full name, date of birth, address and account details

Check you’re using a legitimate website and understand who is collecting your data before entering personal information

Grand Theft Auto and its developer Rockstar Games have been popular targets for attack over recent years.

In 2022, Rockstar Games was hacked by an alleged member of the infamous Lapsus$ collective, with the perpetrator posting around 50 minutes of in-development footage online.

The teen responsible was also linked to a series of extortion attacks on Nvidia, Uber, BT and EE.

In June this year, it was revealed that scammers had registered a number of fake sites falsely claiming to offer early access to GTA 6 in return for crypto payments.
